Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 23, verses 1–11 (part 1 of 2):

Lesson No. 145: Commentary on Verses (1 to 22)

Qad aflaha (Verses 1 to 11)

This is a firm promise, indeed a binding decree from the higher realm, that the believers will attain success. It is Allah's promise, and Allah never breaks His covenant. Moreover, it is Allah's decision, and no one can reject the decision of Allah: that the believers will achieve success in this world as well as in the Hereafter. A believer will attain success individually, and the community of the faithful will also attain success. It is a success that a believer feels in his heart and in his real life, one that contains all the meanings of success known to the world, and also those meanings of success of which even the people of faith may be unaware, which Allah has decreed for them in the future.

Now the question is: who are these believers with whom Allah has made such a firm promise and in advance announced their success and triumph?

Who are the people for whom goodness, help, felicity, divine enabling, and the goods of this world have been written, and for whom the reward of the Hereafter, triumph and salvation have been written, and above all, whose Lord has declared His pleasure with them, and for whom Allah has written success in this world and in that world, and has written what human beings have no knowledge of?

Who are the people who are to inherit Paradise, and in which they will abide forever? These are the people about whom the Speech gives the following details:

1. Those who are humble (khushu') in their prayers.
2. Those who keep away from idle talk (laghw).
3. Those who remain active in giving zakah.
4. Those who guard their private parts, except from their wives and those whom their right hands possess.
5. Those who keep their trusts and covenants.
6. Those who guard their prayers.

Now the thing to consider is: what is the worth of these qualities?

These qualities are different colours of a Muslim's personality. Along with them, a Muslim appears elevated above all people on the horizon of a Muslim humanity. That horizon's standard was set by Muhammad (ﷺ), because he possessed the most excellent character of all creation. Allah himself trained him, gave him the best training, and bore witness to this in His Book.

"Wa innaka la-'ala khuluqin 'azim" (And indeed you are upon an exalted standard of character) — "O Muhammad (ﷺ), you possess a great character." When Hadrat 'A'ishah (رضي الله عنها) was asked about his character, she said: "Kana khuluquhu al-Qur'an" ("His character was the Qur'an"). Then Hadrat 'A'ishah (رضي الله عنها) recited these verses of Surah al-Mu'minun (11) and said: "Such was the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)."

"Alladhina hum fi salatihim khashi'un" (23:2) — "Those who are humble in their prayers."

When they pray, there sits in their hearts the awe that they stand before the Lord of Majesty, with great tranquillity and utmost gentleness. Their movements, their manner of standing and their manner of prostration reflect the fear of Allah and humility. Their souls are filled with the greatness and majesty of Allah. Therefore all other preoccupations disappear from their minds, and all thoughts except presence before Allah fade away. From the veil of their consciousness, their entire environment, their other circumstances and relationships vanish from their body and thought. They are aware of Allah alone, and they feel only the recognition of the Divine Essence. The conscience of these people is purified of all impurities. They set aside for a while all worldly ties; in short, at the time of prayer nothing exists in their sight except the majesty of Allah. Thus the wretched one reaches his true source; a bewildered soul receives the wings of strength; an anxious heart finds a place of rest. At this station, all things, all worldly values and all persons fall from sight, and only that aspect of things remains in view which is connected with Allah.

"Walladhina hum 'ani al-laghwi mu'ridun" (23:3) — "Those who keep away from idle talk."

They keep away from words that are idle, from deeds that are idle, from preferences that are idle, and from thoughts that are idle. That which holds the heart of a believer keeps him away from amusement, frivolity and idle talk. That is, he remains occupied with the remembrance of Allah, keeps thinking about the exalted majesty of Allah, and remains engaged in reflecting upon the signs present in the human self and in the horizons of the universe. Every scene of this universe keeps his mind occupied; his thought constantly contemplates these scenes, and his intuition remains constantly active. He is always engaged in the purification of his heart and vision, purifying himself and cleansing his conscience. Moreover, the change that a believer must bring about in his conduct occupies him day and night. Then he is busy removing the obstacles he encounters on the path of faith. He must carry out the duties of enjoining good and forbidding evil. Then he must also organise his community, and protect it from strife and corruption. A Muslim must, through jihad in the way of Allah, support and defend the Islamic society, and protect it from its opponents and enemies. These are the duties that are obligatory upon a Muslim in every condition. Whether these tasks are individual obligations (fard 'ain) or collective obligations (fard kifayah): if they are carried out properly, they suffice to occupy the whole life of a person in striving, because a human being's lifespan is limited and his strength is also limited. A person will spend this strength either in the above-mentioned tasks, for the growth, progress and reform of humanity, or he will expend this limited power on amusement, play and trivialities. It should be remembered that these duties and all the guidance of the Shari'ah do not prevent a Muslim from occasional lawful recreation, because there is a great difference between lawful recreation and making life utterly meaningless through play and amusement.

"Walladhina hum lil-zakati fa'iluna" (23:4) — "Those who remain active in giving zakah."

After turning towards Allah and distancing themselves from play and a meaningless life, they practise zakah. Zakah is a means of purity for both the human heart and human wealth. Through it, a person's heart is freed from miserliness, and a person sacrifices personal interest, and also resists the whisper of Satan that says, "You will become poor." Furthermore, through zakah that social disease is removed whereby some people become wealthy while others have nothing. In a sense, this is a system of social security and a means of collective support for the poor. Through it, peace, tranquillity and unity can be established among all people and throughout the whole society, and class conflict can be eliminated.

"Walladhina hum li-furujihim hafizun" (23:5) — "Those who guard their private parts."

This is the purity of the soul, the purity of a family, and then the purity of the whole society. Through it, the aim is to save a self, a family and a society from filth. The private parts of a person are protected from illicit and unlawful intercourse. The human heart is protected from debauchery. This is why Islam has prescribed a strict code for sexual gratification.

The fact is that in those societies where free sexual indulgence is customary, their system becomes loose, and such societies fall victim to corruption. In any such society the family system suffers disorder, and the family loses all respect.

Whereas the family is the first unit and the first element of any society, because it is the nursery in which the human seedling grows and gradually develops. Therefore, it is also necessary that peace, tranquillity and purity prevail in the environment of the family, so that this nursery may develop gradually, and parents may cooperate with each other in raising the new human generation. Especially the upbringing of very young children is not possible without the family system.

Furthermore, in a society where free sexual indulgence is unrestrained and shameless, that society is a filthy and foul society. Its individuals are fallen and lacking in resolve, because the standard by which human progress is free of error is that a person's will power dominates all his affairs and all his inclinations. All human natural urges should be organised such that they are pure and clean, and the nursery of human generations formed in that society should not be according to shameful methods. Children should come into this world according to such a pure method that every child knows his father. And it should not happen that in it a female animal takes seed from any male animal, and the animal born afterwards does not know where it came from, how it came, or who brought it.

Here the Holy Qur'an clearly tells them where and how to sow the seed for this nursery, and where to scatter the seeds of life.

"Illa 'ala azwajihim aw ma malakat aymanuhum ghayru malumin" (23:6) — "Except from their wives and those whom their right hands possess; for them there is no blame. As for wives, no explanation is needed," and there is no dispute about it. This is a well-known and legal system. But the matter of "those whom the right hand possesses" requires explanation. We have already discussed the question of slavery at length in volume two of al-Qur'an, in which it was stated that when the Islamic system came, slavery was prevalent as a global system. Likewise, the enslavement of prisoners of war was also an international issue. In the conflict between Islam and unbelief, the enemies of Islam had come onto the field with full material strength; therefore it was not possible for Islam to abolish this system unilaterally, such that Muslims would become captives and slaves of the unbelievers while unbelievers, if taken captive, would be free under that law. The Islamic system, under compulsion, retained the law of enslavement of prisoners of war, while closing the other sources of slavery. And this too only until international law passed a law against slavery.

Accordingly, under this law, some captive women would come into the Islamic camp and would be slaves, and because of their slavery their status was not that of a free married woman; yet Islam permitted intercourse with them only to the person who was their owner, until they attained freedom by the methods that Islam prescribed for the emancipation of slaves, and these methods were numerous.

In the freedom of intercourse with "those whom the right hand possesses" that Islam granted, the natural needs of the captive women themselves were also taken into account, so that captive women would not roam about freely indulging in sexual relations within the Islamic society, as happens today with female prisoners of war, especially after the international agreement against enslaving prisoners of war came into being. Islam continued this law because Islam is opposed to free sexual indulgence and sexual licentiousness. This was a temporary system, and it was for the time until Allah provided arrangements for their freedom, and until these slave women reached the stage of freedom. Islam made such laws that a slave woman can attain freedom by many means. For example, if she bears a son or daughter by her master and the master dies, the slave woman becomes free; or the master himself frees her; or she becomes free through some expiation. Also, a slave woman can become free through mukatabah. Mukatabah is a written agreement in which a slave makes a contract with his master for his freedom. (For further details, see my book Shubuhat hawla al-Islam.)

In any case, slavery was a temporary wartime necessity, and it was such that under international norms, war laws are reciprocal (mithl bil-mithl). That is, just as the enemy nation treats prisoners of war, so will Islam treat them in the same way. In short, making free people slaves was not a permanent principle of the Islamic system, because it was an international necessity.

"Faman ibtaghā warā'a dhalika fa'ulā'ika humu al-'adun" (23:7) — "Whoever seeks beyond that, they are the transgressors."

That is, whoever seeks sexual gratification by any means other than his lawfully married wives and his owned slave-girls will be one who transgresses the lawful boundary. He will fall into what is forbidden. The transgression is that he is gratifying himself by a method other than marriage or jihad. His conscience too will reproach him, because he is grazing in a pasture that is not lawful for him. Furthermore, the offspring resulting from that unlawful intercourse will also be unrestrained like a loose camel, and because of them the whole society will fall victim to corruption. The wolves of that society will be set free, and will tear flesh wherever they wish. All these are forms that Islam disapproves of.

"Walladhina hum li-amanatihim wa 'ahdihim ra'un" (23:8) — "Those who keep their trusts and their covenants."

That is, individually they are guardians of their covenants and pledges, and collectively too, and at the international level also, they are the protectors of covenants and pledges.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran (Urdu translation)) on surah 23, verse 1–11 (part 2 of 2):

The trusts (amanat) include all the responsibilities that are binding upon an individual or a community. The first trust is human nature (fitrat-e-insani). Allah has made human nature extremely straight, and human nature is also in harmony with the order (namus) of the universe. Both of these bear witness, in a just manner, to Allah's oneness (wahdaniyyat) and to His creation, because a single law of nature operates throughout this entire universe, and human nature too is included within it. This unity of the natural order indicates that behind this universe there is one governing will (irada-e-mudabbira) at work. It has been made a duty of the believers that they should not allow this natural disposition of the universe to be changed, because it is a trust with them from Allah, and it is also a just witness to the Lord's majesty. After this, all other trusts follow the same ruling.

The observance of covenants (ahd) also means that first of all one should observe the covenant that is imposed upon human beings by virtue of their fitrah. It is a human duty that, by fitrah, one should recognize Allah alone, that He exists and that He is one; after that covenant come all other pledges and undertakings. The believers observe these commitments. Thus, this is a constant and enduring quality (sifat-e-daimah aur qaimah) of the believers. No system of order in any society can be sound until its members adopt steadfastness (istiqamat), take care of their pledges and promises, and until all the members of that society are content with this shared system of life, so that all people may attain peace and tranquility and live with confidence.

"Wallazina hum ala salawatihim yuhafizun" (23:9): "Those who guard their prayers." They never delay their prayers beyond their time, nor do they waste them. Likewise, they do not diminish the quality of their prayers. They fully perform the obligatory parts (fara'id), the sunnah and the recommended acts (mustahabbat) of these prayers. They offer their prayers with complete postures (arkan) and etiquette (adab). Their prayers are living prayers, and with full attention they become absorbed in them; their spirit and their inner perception receive a good effect from the prayers. Prayer is in fact a connection between the servant and the Lord. Whoever does not guard the prayer, in reality cuts off this connection between himself and his Lord. And such a person then also does not maintain good relations with the rest of mankind. The description of the qualities of the believers begins with the mention of prayer and ends with the mention of prayer. The purpose is to show that after faith (iman) and Islam, prayer is the most important obligation. Here emphasis is laid upon performing prayer with all its qualities and directing one's full attention toward Allah, for in Islam there is prayer at the beginning and prayer at the end.

These are the qualities of the believers for whom Allah has written success (falah). These are the characteristics that determine what the features of the life of the believers are and what kind of life the believers should lead. That is, a life worthy of a human being to whom dignity (karamat) and nobility (sharaf) over all creation has been granted. Neither should one enjoy life in such a way that one merely lives like animals without further advancing one's life, nor should one enjoy life in the manner in which animals enjoy it, nor eat and drink in the manner in which animals eat and drink.

But despite this all-encompassing progress of the world, that progress and perfection worthy of the believers cannot be attained in this world; therefore Allah, moving man further forward on the path of progress, brought him to the highest stages of progress and perfection, namely the Paradise of Firdaws. The believers will always remain at these lofty stages of progress and perfection. There they will have no fear or danger, and there they will remain in unending peace and tranquility.

"Ula'ika humul warithun (10). Allazina yaritunal Firdausa hum fiha khalidun" (23:10-11): "It is those who are the inheritors, who will inherit Firdaws and will abide therein forever." This is the ultimate goal that has been written for the believers. Beyond it, a believer has no other objective, and after attaining it, he has no other objective left for which he might yearn.

One important quality of the believers is that they reflect upon the proofs of faith found within their own souls. First of all, they should consider the reality of their own existence and its growth: from what small germ the beginning of their personality arose, and then what the condition of resurrection after death and of the life of the Hereafter will be. What is the nature of the connection between these two lives, the worldly and the otherworldly?

1. Those who are humble (khushu') in their prayers.
2. Those who keep away from idle talk (laghw).
3. Those who remain active in giving zakah.
4. Those who guard their private parts, except from their wives and those whom their right hands possess.
5. Those who keep their trusts and covenants.
6. Those who guard their prayers.

Allah himself trained him, gave him the best training, and bore witness to this in His Book.

Then Hadrat 'A'ishah (رضي الله عنها) recited these verses of Surah al-Mu'minun (11) and said: "Such was the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)."

"Alladhina hum fi salatihim khashi'un" (23:2) — "Those who are humble in their prayers."

When they pray, there sits in their hearts the awe that they stand before the Lord of Majesty, with great tranquillity and utmost gentleness. Their movements, their manner of standing and their manner of prostration reflect the fear of Allah and humility. Their souls are filled with the greatness and majesty of Allah. Therefore all other preoccupations disappear from their minds, and all thoughts except presence before Allah fade away. From the veil of their consciousness, their entire environment, their other circumstances and relationships vanish from their body and thought. They are aware of Allah alone, and they feel only the recognition of the Divine Essence. The conscience of these people is purified of all impurities. They set aside for a while all worldly ties; in short, at the time of prayer nothing exists in their sight except the majesty of Allah. Thus the wretched one reaches his true source; a bewildered soul receives the wings of strength; an anxious heart finds a place of rest. At this station, all things, all worldly values and all persons fall from sight, and only that aspect of things remains in view which is connected with Allah.

"Walladhina hum 'ani al-laghwi mu'ridun" (23:3) — "Those who keep away from idle talk."

They keep away from words that are idle, from deeds that are idle, from preferences that are idle, and from thoughts that are idle. That is, he remains occupied with the remembrance of Allah, keeps thinking about the exalted majesty of Allah, and remains engaged in reflecting upon the signs present in the human self and in the horizons of the universe. Every scene of this universe keeps his mind occupied; his thought constantly contemplates these scenes, and his intuition remains constantly active. He is always engaged in the purification of his heart and vision, purifying himself and cleansing his conscience. Moreover, the change that a believer must bring about in his conduct occupies him day and night. Then he is busy removing the obstacles he encounters on the path of faith. He must carry out the duties of enjoining good and forbidding evil. Then he must also organise his community, and protect it from strife and corruption. A Muslim must, through jihad in the way of Allah, support and defend the Islamic society, and protect it from its opponents and enemies. These are the duties that are obligatory upon a Muslim in every condition. Whether these tasks are individual obligations (fard 'ain) or collective obligations (fard kifayah): if they are carried out properly, they suffice to occupy the whole life of a person in striving, because a human being's lifespan is limited and his strength is also limited. "Walladhina hum lil-zakati fa'iluna" (23:4) — "Those who remain active in giving zakah."

After turning towards Allah and distancing themselves from play and a meaningless life, they practise zakah. Zakah is a means of purity for both the human heart and human wealth. Through it, a person's heart is freed from miserliness, and a person sacrifices personal interest, and also resists the whisper of Satan that says, "You will become poor." Furthermore, through zakah that social disease is removed whereby some people become wealthy while others have nothing. In a sense, this is a system of social security and a means of collective support for the poor. Through it, peace, tranquillity and unity can be established among all people and throughout the whole society, and class conflict can be eliminated.

"Walladhina hum li-furujihim hafizun" (23:5) — "Those who guard their private parts."

The private parts of a person are protected from illicit and unlawful intercourse. The human heart is protected from debauchery. This is why Islam has prescribed a strict code for sexual gratification.

The fact is that in those societies where free sexual indulgence is customary, their system becomes loose, and such societies fall victim to corruption. In any such society the family system suffers disorder, and the family loses all respect.

Whereas the family is the first unit and the first element of any society, because it is the nursery in which the human seedling grows and gradually develops. Therefore, it is also necessary that peace, tranquillity and purity prevail in the environment of the family, so that this nursery may develop gradually, and parents may cooperate with each other in raising the new human generation. "Alladhina hum fi salatihim khashi'un" (23:2) — "Those who are humble in their prayers."

When they pray, there sits in their hearts the awe that they stand before the Lord of Majesty, with great tranquillity and utmost gentleness. Their movements, their manner of standing and their manner of prostration reflect the fear of Allah and humility. Their souls are filled with the greatness and majesty of Allah. Therefore all other preoccupations disappear from their minds, and all thoughts except presence before Allah fade away. From the veil of their consciousness, their entire environment, their other circumstances and relationships vanish from their body and thought. They are aware of Allah alone, and they feel only the recognition of the Divine Essence. The conscience of these people is purified of all impurities. They set aside for a while all worldly ties; in short, at the time of prayer nothing exists in their sight except the majesty of Allah. Thus the wretched one reaches his true source; a bewildered soul receives the wings of strength; an anxious heart finds a place of rest. "Walladhina hum 'ani al-laghwi mu'ridun" (23:3) — "Those who keep away from idle talk."

"Walladhina hum lil-zakati fa'iluna" (23:4) — "Those who remain active in giving zakah."

Furthermore, through zakah that social disease is removed whereby some people become wealthy while others have nothing. Both of these bear witness, in a just manner, to Allah's oneness (wahdaniyyat) and to His creation, because a single law of nature operates throughout this entire universe, and human nature too is included within it. This unity of the natural order indicates that behind this universe there is one governing will (irada-e-mudabbira) at work. It has been made a duty of the believers that they should not allow this natural disposition of the universe to be changed, because it is a trust with them from Allah, and it is also a just witness to the Lord's majesty. After this, all other trusts follow the same ruling.

The observance of covenants (ahd) also means that first of all one should observe the covenant that is imposed upon human beings by virtue of their fitrah. It is a human duty that, by fitrah, one should recognize Allah alone, that He exists and that He is one; after that covenant come all other pledges and undertakings. The believers observe these commitments. Thus, this is a constant and enduring quality (sifat-e-daimah aur qaimah) of the believers. No system of order in any society can be sound until its members adopt steadfastness (istiqamat), take care of their pledges and promises, and until all the members of that society are content with this shared system of life, so that all people may attain peace and tranquility and live with confidence.

"Wallazina hum ala salawatihim yuhafizun" (23:9): "Those who guard their prayers." They never delay their prayers beyond their time, nor do they waste them. Likewise, they do not diminish the quality of their prayers. They fully perform the obligatory parts (fara'id), the sunnah and the recommended acts (mustahabbat) of these prayers. They offer their prayers with complete postures (arkan) and etiquette (adab). Their prayers are living prayers, and with full attention they become absorbed in them; their spirit and their inner perception receive a good effect from the prayers. Prayer is in fact a connection between the servant and the Lord. Whoever does not guard the prayer, in reality cuts off this connection between himself and his Lord. And such a person then also does not maintain good relations with the rest of mankind. The description of the qualities of the believers begins with the mention of prayer and ends with the mention of prayer. The purpose is to show that after faith (iman) and Islam, prayer is the most important obligation. Here emphasis is laid upon performing prayer with all its qualities and directing one's full attention toward Allah, for in Islam there is prayer at the beginning and prayer at the end.

These are the characteristics that determine what the features of the life of the believers are and what kind of life the believers should lead. Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 23, verses 1–11 (part 1 of 2):

Lesson No. 145: Commentary on Verses (1 to 22)

Qad aflaha (Verses 1 to 11)

This is a firm promise, indeed a binding decree from the higher realm, that the believers will attain success. It is Allah's promise, and Allah never breaks His covenant. Moreover, it is Allah's decision, and no one can reject the decision of Allah: that the believers will achieve success in this world as well as in the Hereafter. A believer will attain success individually, and the community of the faithful will also attain success. It is a success that a believer feels in his heart and in his real life, one that contains all the meanings of success known to the world, and also those meanings of success of which even the people of faith may be unaware, which Allah has decreed for them in the future.

Now the question is: who are these believers with whom Allah has made such a firm promise and in advance announced their success and triumph?

Who are the people for whom goodness, help, felicity, divine enabling, and the goods of this world have been written, and for whom the reward of the Hereafter, triumph and salvation have been written, and above all, whose Lord has declared His pleasure with them, and for whom Allah has written success in this world and in that world, and has written what human beings have no knowledge of?

Who are the people who are to inherit Paradise, and in which they will abide forever? These are the people about whom the Speech gives the following details:

1. Those who are humble (khushu') in their prayers.
2. Those who keep away from idle talk (laghw).
3. Those who remain active in giving zakah.
4. Those who guard their private parts, except from their wives and those whom their right hands possess.
5. Those who keep their trusts and covenants.
6. Those who guard their prayers.

Now the thing to consider is: what is the worth of these qualities?

These qualities are different colours of a Muslim's personality. Along with them, a Muslim appears elevated above all people on the horizon of a Muslim humanity. That horizon's standard was set by Muhammad (ﷺ), because he possessed the most excellent character of all creation. Allah himself trained him, gave him the best training, and bore witness to this in His Book.

"Wa innaka la-'ala khuluqin 'azim" (And indeed you are upon an exalted standard of character) — "O Muhammad (ﷺ), you possess a great character." When Hadrat 'A'ishah (رضي الله عنها) was asked about his character, she said: "Kana khuluquhu al-Qur'an" ("His character was the Qur'an"). Then Hadrat 'A'ishah (رضي الله عنها) recited these verses of Surah al-Mu'minun (11) and said: "Such was the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)."

"Alladhina hum fi salatihim khashi'un" (23:2) — "Those who are humble in their prayers."

When they pray, there sits in their hearts the awe that they stand before the Lord of Majesty, with great tranquillity and utmost gentleness. Their movements, their manner of standing and their manner of prostration reflect the fear of Allah and humility. Their souls are filled with the greatness and majesty of Allah. Therefore all other preoccupations disappear from their minds, and all thoughts except presence before Allah fade away. From the veil of their consciousness, their entire environment, their other circumstances and relationships vanish from their body and thought. They are aware of Allah alone, and they feel only the recognition of the Divine Essence. The conscience of these people is purified of all impurities. They set aside for a while all worldly ties; in short, at the time of prayer nothing exists in their sight except the majesty of Allah. Thus the wretched one reaches his true source; a bewildered soul receives the wings of strength; an anxious heart finds a place of rest. At this station, all things, all worldly values and all persons fall from sight, and only that aspect of things remains in view which is connected with Allah.

"Walladhina hum 'ani al-laghwi mu'ridun" (23:3) — "Those who keep away from idle talk."

They keep away from words that are idle, from deeds that are idle, from preferences that are idle, and from thoughts that are idle. That which holds the heart of a believer keeps him away from amusement, frivolity and idle talk. That is, he remains occupied with the remembrance of Allah, keeps thinking about the exalted majesty of Allah, and remains engaged in reflecting upon the signs present in the human self and in the horizons of the universe. Every scene of this universe keeps his mind occupied; his thought constantly contemplates these scenes, and his intuition remains constantly active. He is always engaged in the purification of his heart and vision, purifying himself and cleansing his conscience. Moreover, the change that a believer must bring about in his conduct occupies him day and night. Then he is busy removing the obstacles he encounters on the path of faith. He must carry out the duties of enjoining good and forbidding evil. Then he must also organise his community, and protect it from strife and corruption. A Muslim must, through jihad in the way of Allah, support and defend the Islamic society, and protect it from its opponents and enemies. These are the duties that are obligatory upon a Muslim in every condition. Whether these tasks are individual obligations (fard 'ain) or collective obligations (fard kifayah): if they are carried out properly, they suffice to occupy the whole life of a person in striving, because a human being's lifespan is limited and his strength is also limited. A person will spend this strength either in the above-mentioned tasks, for the growth, progress and reform of humanity, or he will expend this limited power on amusement, play and trivialities. It should be remembered that these duties and all the guidance of the Shari'ah do not prevent a Muslim from occasional lawful recreation, because there is a great difference between lawful recreation and making life utterly meaningless through play and amusement.

"Walladhina hum lil-zakati fa'iluna" (23:4) — "Those who remain active in giving zakah."

After turning towards Allah and distancing themselves from play and a meaningless life, they practise zakah. Zakah is a means of purity for both the human heart and human wealth. Through it, a person's heart is freed from miserliness, and a person sacrifices personal interest, and also resists the whisper of Satan that says, "You will become poor." Furthermore, through zakah that social disease is removed whereby some people become wealthy while others have nothing. In a sense, this is a system of social security and a means of collective support for the poor. Through it, peace, tranquillity and unity can be established among all people and throughout the whole society, and class conflict can be eliminated.

"Walladhina hum li-furujihim hafizun" (23:5) — "Those who guard their private parts."

This is the purity of the soul, the purity of a family, and then the purity of the whole society. Through it, the aim is to save a self, a family and a society from filth. The private parts of a person are protected from illicit and unlawful intercourse. The human heart is protected from debauchery. This is why Islam has prescribed a strict code for sexual gratification.

The fact is that in those societies where free sexual indulgence is customary, their system becomes loose, and such societies fall victim to corruption. In any such society the family system suffers disorder, and the family loses all respect.

Whereas the family is the first unit and the first element of any society, because it is the nursery in which the human seedling grows and gradually develops. Therefore, it is also necessary that peace, tranquillity and purity prevail in the environment of the family, so that this nursery may develop gradually, and parents may cooperate with each other in raising the new human generation. Especially the upbringing of very young children is not possible without the family system.

Furthermore, in a society where free sexual indulgence is unrestrained and shameless, that society is a filthy and foul society. Its individuals are fallen and lacking in resolve, because the standard by which human progress is free of error is that a person's will power dominates all his affairs and all his inclinations. All human natural urges should be organised such that they are pure and clean, and the nursery of human generations formed in that society should not be according to shameful methods. Children should come into this world according to such a pure method that every child knows his father. And it should not happen that in it a female animal takes seed from any male animal, and the animal born afterwards does not know where it came from, how it came, or who brought it.

Here the Holy Qur'an clearly tells them where and how to sow the seed for this nursery, and where to scatter the seeds of life.

"Illa 'ala azwajihim aw ma malakat aymanuhum ghayru malumin" (23:6) — "Except from their wives and those whom their right hands possess; for them there is no blame. As for wives, no explanation is needed," and there is no dispute about it. This is a well-known and legal system. But the matter of "those whom the right hand possesses" requires explanation. We have already discussed the question of slavery at length in volume two of al-Qur'an, in which it was stated that when the Islamic system came, slavery was prevalent as a global system. Likewise, the enslavement of prisoners of war was also an international issue. In the conflict between Islam and unbelief, the enemies of Islam had come onto the field with full material strength; therefore it was not possible for Islam to abolish this system unilaterally, such that Muslims would become captives and slaves of the unbelievers while unbelievers, if taken captive, would be free under that law. The Islamic system, under compulsion, retained the law of enslavement of prisoners of war, while closing the other sources of slavery. And this too only until international law passed a law against slavery.

Accordingly, under this law, some captive women would come into the Islamic camp and would be slaves, and because of their slavery their status was not that of a free married woman; yet Islam permitted intercourse with them only to the person who was their owner, until they attained freedom by the methods that Islam prescribed for the emancipation of slaves, and these methods were numerous.

In the freedom of intercourse with "those whom the right hand possesses" that Islam granted, the natural needs of the captive women themselves were also taken into account, so that captive women would not roam about freely indulging in sexual relations within the Islamic society, as happens today with female prisoners of war, especially after the international agreement against enslaving prisoners of war came into being. Islam continued this law because Islam is opposed to free sexual indulgence and sexual licentiousness. This was a temporary system, and it was for the time until Allah provided arrangements for their freedom, and until these slave women reached the stage of freedom. Islam made such laws that a slave woman can attain freedom by many means. For example, if she bears a son or daughter by her master and the master dies, the slave woman becomes free; or the master himself frees her; or she becomes free through some expiation. Also, a slave woman can become free through mukatabah. Mukatabah is a written agreement in which a slave makes a contract with his master for his freedom. (For further details, see my book Shubuhat hawla al-Islam.)

In any case, slavery was a temporary wartime necessity, and it was such that under international norms, war laws are reciprocal (mithl bil-mithl). That is, just as the enemy nation treats prisoners of war, so will Islam treat them in the same way. In short, making free people slaves was not a permanent principle of the Islamic system, because it was an international necessity.

"Faman ibtaghā warā'a dhalika fa'ulā'ika humu al-'adun" (23:7) — "Whoever seeks beyond that, they are the transgressors."

That is, whoever seeks sexual gratification by any means other than his lawfully married wives and his owned slave-girls will be one who transgresses the lawful boundary. He will fall into what is forbidden. The transgression is that he is gratifying himself by a method other than marriage or jihad. His conscience too will reproach him, because he is grazing in a pasture that is not lawful for him. Furthermore, the offspring resulting from that unlawful intercourse will also be unrestrained like a loose camel, and because of them the whole society will fall victim to corruption. The wolves of that society will be set free, and will tear flesh wherever they wish. All these are forms that Islam disapproves of.

"Walladhina hum li-amanatihim wa 'ahdihim ra'un" (23:8) — "Those who keep their trusts and their covenants."

That is, individually they are guardians of their covenants and pledges, and collectively too, and at the international level also, they are the protectors of covenants and pledges.

"Alladhina hum fi salatihim khashi'un" (23:2) — "Those who are humble in their prayers."

Therefore all other preoccupations disappear from their minds, and all thoughts except presence before Allah fade away. "Walladhina hum 'ani al-laghwi mu'ridun" (23:3) — "Those who keep away from idle talk."

That is, he remains occupied with the remembrance of Allah, keeps thinking about the exalted majesty of Allah, and remains engaged in reflecting upon the signs present in the human self and in the horizons of the universe. Every scene of this universe keeps his mind occupied; his thought constantly contemplates these scenes, and his intuition remains constantly active. He is always engaged in the purification of his heart and vision, purifying himself and cleansing his conscience. Moreover, the change that a believer must bring about in his conduct occupies him day and night. Then he is busy removing the obstacles he encounters on the path of faith. He must carry out the duties of enjoining good and forbidding evil. Then he must also organise his community, and protect it from strife and corruption. A Muslim must, through jihad in the way of Allah, support and defend the Islamic society, and protect it from its opponents and enemies. These are the duties that are obligatory upon a Muslim in every condition. It should be remembered that these duties and all the guidance of the Shari'ah do not prevent a Muslim from occasional lawful recreation, because there is a great difference between lawful recreation and making life utterly meaningless through play and amusement.

"Walladhina hum lil-zakati fa'iluna" (23:4) — "Those who remain active in giving zakah."

Furthermore, through zakah that social disease is removed whereby some people become wealthy while others have nothing. This is the purity of the soul, the purity of a family, and then the purity of the whole society. Through it, the aim is to save a self, a family and a society from filth. The private parts of a person are protected from illicit and unlawful intercourse. The human heart is protected from debauchery. This is why Islam has prescribed a strict code for sexual gratification.

The fact is that in those societies where free sexual indulgence is customary, their system becomes loose, and such societies fall victim to corruption. In any such society the family system suffers disorder, and the family loses all respect.

Likewise, the enslavement of prisoners of war was also an international issue. In the conflict between Islam and unbelief, the enemies of Islam had come onto the field with full material strength; therefore it was not possible for Islam to abolish this system unilaterally, such that Muslims would become captives and slaves of the unbelievers while unbelievers, if taken captive, would be free under that law. The Islamic system, under compulsion, retained the law of enslavement of prisoners of war, while closing the other sources of slavery. And this too only until international law passed a law against slavery.

Accordingly, under this law, some captive women would come into the Islamic camp and would be slaves, and because of their slavery their status was not that of a free married woman; yet Islam permitted intercourse with them only to the person who was their owner, until they attained freedom by the methods that Islam prescribed for the emancipation of slaves, and these methods were numerous.

In the freedom of intercourse with "those whom the right hand possesses" that Islam granted, the natural needs of the captive women themselves were also taken into account, so that captive women would not roam about freely indulging in sexual relations within the Islamic society, as happens today with female prisoners of war, especially after the international agreement against enslaving prisoners of war came into being. Islam continued this law because Islam is opposed to free sexual indulgence and sexual licentiousness. This was a temporary system, and it was for the time until Allah provided arrangements for their freedom, and until these slave women reached the stage of freedom. Islam made such laws that a slave woman can attain freedom by many means. For example, if she bears a son or daughter by her master and the master dies, the slave woman becomes free; or the master himself frees her; or she becomes free through some expiation. Also, a slave woman can become free through mukatabah. Mukatabah is a written agreement in which a slave makes a contract with his master for his freedom. (For further details, see my book Shubuhat hawla al-Islam.)

In any case, slavery was a temporary wartime necessity, and it was such that under international norms, war laws are reciprocal (mithl bil-mithl). That is, just as the enemy nation treats prisoners of war, so will Islam treat them in the same way. In short, making free people slaves was not a permanent principle of the Islamic system, because it was an international necessity.

Lesson No. 145: Commentary on Verses (1 to 22)

Qad aflaha (Verses 1 to 11)

This is a firm promise, indeed a binding decree from the higher realm, that the believers will attain success. It is Allah's promise, and Allah never breaks His covenant. Moreover, it is Allah's decision, and no one can reject the decision of Allah: that the believers will achieve success in this world as well as in the Hereafter. A believer will attain success individually, and the community of the faithful will also attain success. It is a success that a believer feels in his heart and in his real life, one that contains all the meanings of success known to the world, and also those meanings of success of which even the people of faith may be unaware, which Allah has decreed for them in the future.

Now the question is: who are these believers with whom Allah has made such a firm promise and in advance announced their success and triumph?

Who are the people for whom goodness, help, felicity, divine enabling, and the goods of this world have been written, and for whom the reward of the Hereafter, triumph and salvation have been written, and above all, whose Lord has declared His pleasure with them, and for whom Allah has written success in this world and in that world, and has written what human beings have no knowledge of?

Who are the people who are to inherit Paradise, and in which they will abide forever? These are the people about whom the Speech gives the following details:

1. Those who are humble (khushu') in their prayers.
2. Those who keep away from idle talk (laghw).
3. Those who remain active in giving zakah.
4. Those who guard their private parts, except from their wives and those whom their right hands possess.
5. Those who keep their trusts and covenants.
6. Those who guard their prayers.

Now the thing to consider is: what is the worth of these qualities?

These qualities are different colours of a Muslim's personality. Along with them, a Muslim appears elevated above all people on the horizon of a Muslim humanity. That horizon's standard was set by Muhammad (ﷺ), because he possessed the most excellent character of all creation. Allah himself trained him, gave him the best training, and bore witness to this in His Book.

"Alladhina hum fi salatihim khashi'un" (23:2) — "Those who are humble in their prayers."

When they pray, there sits in their hearts the awe that they stand before the Lord of Majesty, with great tranquillity and utmost gentleness. Their movements, their manner of standing and their manner of prostration reflect the fear of Allah and humility. Their souls are filled with the greatness and majesty of Allah. Therefore all other preoccupations disappear from their minds, and all thoughts except presence before Allah fade away. From the veil of their consciousness, their entire environment, their other circumstances and relationships vanish from their body and thought. They are aware of Allah alone, and they feel only the recognition of the Divine Essence. The conscience of these people is purified of all impurities. They set aside for a while all worldly ties; in short, at the time of prayer nothing exists in their sight except the majesty of Allah. Thus the wretched one reaches his true source; a bewildered soul receives the wings of strength; an anxious heart finds a place of rest. At this station, all things, all worldly values and all persons fall from sight, and only that aspect of things remains in view which is connected with Allah.

"Walladhina hum 'ani al-laghwi mu'ridun" (23:3) — "Those who keep away from idle talk."

They keep away from words that are idle, from deeds that are idle, from preferences that are idle, and from thoughts that are idle. That which holds the heart of a believer keeps him away from amusement, frivolity and idle talk. That is, he remains occupied with the remembrance of Allah, keeps thinking about the exalted majesty of Allah, and remains engaged in reflecting upon the signs present in the human self and in the horizons of the universe. Every scene of this universe keeps his mind occupied; his thought constantly contemplates these scenes, and his intuition remains constantly active. He is always engaged in the purification of his heart and vision, purifying himself and cleansing his conscience. Moreover, the change that a believer must bring about in his conduct occupies him day and night. Then he is busy removing the obstacles he encounters on the path of faith. He must carry out the duties of enjoining good and forbidding evil. Then he must also organise his community, and protect it from strife and corruption. A Muslim must, through jihad in the way of Allah, support and defend the Islamic society, and protect it from its opponents and enemies. These are the duties that are obligatory upon a Muslim in every condition. Whether these tasks are individual obligations (fard 'ain) or collective obligations (fard kifayah): if they are carried out properly, they suffice to occupy the whole life of a person in striving, because a human being's lifespan is limited and his strength is also limited. A person will spend this strength either in the above-mentioned tasks, for the growth, progress and reform of humanity, or he will expend this limited power on amusement, play and trivialities. It should be remembered that these duties and all the guidance of the Shari'ah do not prevent a Muslim from occasional lawful recreation, because there is a great difference between lawful recreation and making life utterly meaningless through play and amusement.

"Walladhina hum lil-zakati fa'iluna" (23:4) — "Those who remain active in giving zakah."

After turning towards Allah and distancing themselves from play and a meaningless life, they practise zakah. Zakah is a means of purity for both the human heart and human wealth. Furthermore, through zakah that social disease is removed whereby some people become wealthy while others have nothing. Therefore, it is also necessary that peace, tranquillity and purity prevail in the environment of the family, so that this nursery may develop gradually, and parents may cooperate with each other in raising the new human generation. Especially the upbringing of very young children is not possible without the family system.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 23, verses 12–14:

ولقد تبعثون (12 تا 16)

This manner of creation, this orderly manner of development, and the continuity found within it. First of all, it shows that this whole system has a Creator, and from this it becomes known that this entire process accords with His purposeful will and design. This extremely intricate process does not simply happen by chance, nor does this whole process occur merely by accident without any will and planning. In particular, consider this aspect: in this entire system of events, this chain is never broken. The system of human creation could rationally take several other forms, yet this method never admits of change. This aspect especially demonstrates that there is a specific will behind this system.

This gradual development of human life, with its continuity, appears to be a marvel, and it can be resolved only in this way: that a person, in accordance with this surah, straightforwardly comes to believe in Allah.

This alone is the way by which one can be given the conception of bringing this creation and this development to their perfection. Only in the case of faith in Allah can the life of this world and the Hereafter be meaningful and purposeful. After the description of the attributes of the believers, why has the account of the stages of this wondrous development of life been brought here?

ولقد خلقنا الانسان من سللۃ من طین (23 : 12) "We created man from an extract of clay, then We made him a drop of fluid placed in a secure place." This verse describes the manner of human development with great precision. It shows that man reaches his present human form after passing through several stages. First he progressed from clay to man; mud, as it were, is the first stage of human creation, and man in his present form is the final stage of this process of creation. This is the reality that the Holy Qur'an expounds. We do not wish to confirm this process of human creation by those scientific observations which have observed this process of creation in great detail, showing how human life develops.

The Holy Qur'an has described how intricate creation is. The noteworthy point is how great the transformation is from mud to the creation of man. The Holy Qur'an has not given further details, because the purpose of the Qur'an is fulfilled by mentioning these broad stages of creation. As for present scientific observations, they set before us a very detailed account of the stages of development, so that they may explain in detail the stages from mud to the complete creation of man. Scientists' observations may be correct, and sometimes they also make erroneous observations. Today they state more stages, and tomorrow they reduce them, because observational instruments undergo changes from day to day.

The Qur'an sometimes describes these stages briefly and sometimes gives their details. Sometimes it contains just this phrase:

وبدا خلق الانسان من طین (32 : 7) "The initial creation of man was from clay." Now there is no mention of stages in this, while in the verse where details are given, it says:

من سللۃ من طین (23 : 12) "In the other verse, brevity has been employed." As for how man progressed from clay to his present complete state with continuity, the Qur'an has not given its details, and as we have given details elsewhere, these matters are not included among the aims of the Qur'an. The stages of life that the Qur'an has described may accord with scientific observations or may contradict them. It is also possible that this process occurred through some unknown means that man has not yet discovered, or that there are some factors that are beyond human knowledge. But the view with which the Qur'an regards man and the purposes for which these other scientific theories observe him are as different as earth from heaven. The Qur'an declares man to be a most honoured and chosen creature. It says that into this being Allah breathed His spirit, and it was this spirit that made him a human being from clay, and gave him two distinctive qualities by which he was called a human and was distinguished from animals. Thus the Qur'an's viewpoint regarding man is entirely distinct from that of materialists, and the word of Allah is truer than that of all people.

(See al-Insan bayn al-Maddiyya wal-Islam by Muhammad Qutb.) This is the original creation of the human species from an extract of clay. As for the subsequent line of human progeny, its manner is entirely different and is a well-known and observed method.

ثم جعلنہ نطفۃ فی قرار مکین (23 : 13) "Then We made him a drop of fluid in a secure place." Allah created the human species (Adam) from an extract of clay. As for the chain of procreation, Allah has set it in motion from a drop of water. This drop of water emerges from the male loins. It settles in the womb of the mother. It is an extremely tiny point of water, indeed one cell among thousands, and within this drop of water these cells are present in thousands.

فی قرار مکین (23 : 13) "in a secure place." This drop, upon reaching the womb, settles between the bones of the womb in such a place that the movements of the body have no effect upon it. It is a place which, while the back and stomach of a person receive jolts, blows, movements and impacts, is protected from them.

The Qur'an declares this point to be a stage of human creation; from this point, man becomes a complete human being. This is a scientific fact, yet it is a wondrous and worthy-of-reflection fact. When We reduce this great-bodied human being to this point, and within that point all the human characteristics are present, then from within a complete human being there continue to be created other such genes. This is a wondrous system of the chain of creation.

From this point, man then becomes an 'alaqa, that is, a clot of blood. In this stage, the male sperm combines with the female ovum, and initially this is a fine point suspended from the womb of the mother. This point receives nourishment from the blood of the mother's womb. From 'alaqa it then becomes al-mudgha, a "lump of flesh," in the form of a morsel. In the form of a morsel, this point is now somewhat larger. Now it is a piece of flesh. It is a thick piece of blood.

This small creature travels upon its path. It does not change its course, nor does it move away from its road. Its movement is orderly and arranged, and it accords with the law that Allah has set in advance, that is, in accordance with Allah's providence and decree. After this comes the stage of bones.

فخلقنا المضغۃ عظما (23 : 13) "Then We made the lump into bones." And after this stage came the stage in which flesh was clothed over the bones.

فکسونا العظم لحما (23 : 31) "Then We clothed the bones with flesh." On reading and then observing these stages, a person is astonished that the Qur'an has described these stages in such detail, which scientists observed much later. Later, scientists came to know that the cells of bones are different, and the cells of flesh are different, and it was established beyond doubt that within the embryo the bone cells are formed first, and afterwards flesh cells are laid upon them, and until the bone cells are complete, the flesh cells are not perfected, and afterwards the skeleton of the embryo is formed. This is an amazing reality, which the Qur'an records.

فخلقنا المضغۃ عظما فکسونا العظم لحما (23 : 14) "Then We made the lump into bones, and then clothed the bones with flesh." ثم انشانہ خلقا اخر (23 : 14) "Then We brought it into being as another creation." And this creation is man. It possesses distinctive characteristics. In the beginning the embryo of a human and that of an animal appear alike in physical structure, but at the end the human embryo assumes the form of a different creation. It is an honoured and distinguished creation, and it possesses a tremendous capacity for evolution and advancement. The embryo of an animal remains at the level of an animal. It cannot acquire human characteristics, and does not reach the perfections that man reaches.

The fact is that the human embryo has been given specific and particular characteristics, and it is these characteristics that set man on the path of humanity in later times. Thus man becomes "another" creation, and this happens at the time when this embryo is in the final period of its development. The animal, in its final period, remains behind man because it has not been given human characteristics. Accordingly, it is not possible for any animal to advance beyond its animal station and, progressing gradually, become a human being, as materialist theory's adherents believe. Rather, man, by virtue of his human characteristics, halts at a certain station and becomes "another creation," and becomes capable of bearing the responsibilities he is to discharge on this earth. This difference is due to the distinctive characteristics that Allah has given to man. In this matter, the view that animals have advanced, progressing step by step to the level of human beings, is entirely false.

The theory of evolution rests on a concept contrary to the Islamic view. This theory assumes that present-day man is a stage of animal evolution, and that an animal can also progress and become a human being. But the actual state of affairs is that this theory is clearly seen to be mere hypothesis and falsehood. An animal can never possess human characteristics. It always remains within its limits and cannot advance beyond them. It is possible that within a species, some animal may develop in form, as Darwin claims. But every species remains within its species limits; it cannot change its species characteristics, because the characteristics of every animal species are distinct and were given to it by some external power, whereas the human species is of a completely separate nature and has characteristics which Allah's power has bestowed for certain specific purposes.

فتبرک اللہ احسن الخلقین (23 : 14) "So blessed is Allah, the best of creators." He who has placed within the human embryo this capacity moves forward according to this manner of development, in accordance with an automatic system, following a highly intricate divine custom (sunnah) in which there is no change, and no stage of it is dropped, until man reaches the appointed level of perfection and development.

People call the discoveries of science a miracle and express wonder on hearing them, especially when man produces a device or machine that operates by an automatic method and works without human intervention. Do these people not look at this embryo, which proceeds through its various stages in a highly automatic manner? Apparently, in passing through these stages, no one is seen who is causing it to pass through them. When it enters from one stage into another, its very nature also undergoes a complete change. Then it is seen that within it a change has come about between those two stages. People see these transformations and events day and night, yet they pass on with their eyes closed; their hearts and minds do not reflect upon this vast automatic system. Why is this? Because we have become accustomed to this system, although in itself it is an astonishing system. Merely reflecting on this intricate creation of man is sufficient for human guidance, in which all its characteristics and all its features are present within that small point which is so tiny that a person cannot see it without a microscope. All these characteristics and all these features gradually grow and, passing through their various stages, come again before our eyes. When the person is in the form of a child, the human characteristics begin to appear. Then every child inherits, along with the general human characteristics, the particular characteristics of its parents, and both kinds of characteristics are concentrated within that small point. In short, this process which nature repeats day and night before us and among us is sufficient to open a person's eyes, and within it there is vast material for human reflection.

Now the context advances one step further to bring this journey of life to its conclusion. Now there is mention of a new stage of life. Because this life, whose creation was from clay, does not end in this world, since it is not mere clay but a mixture of spirit has been put into it, it must therefore proceed beyond this. Since a spirit has been breathed into this life from the higher realm, its final destination is not this physical stage. There are other worlds beyond this nearer stage of blood and flesh. Thus the final stage of life comes into view.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 23, verses 12–14:

ولقد تبعثون (12 تا 16)

This manner of creation, this orderly manner of development, and the continuity found within it. First of all, it shows that this whole system has a Creator, and from this it becomes known that this entire process accords with His purposeful will and design. This extremely intricate process does not simply happen by chance, nor does this whole process occur merely by accident without any will and planning. In particular, consider this aspect: in this entire system of events, this chain is never broken. The system of human creation could rationally take several other forms, yet this method never admits of change. This aspect especially demonstrates that there is a specific will behind this system.

This gradual development of human life, with its continuity, appears to be a marvel, and it can be resolved only in this way: that a person, in accordance with this surah, straightforwardly comes to believe in Allah.

This alone is the way by which one can be given the conception of bringing this creation and this development to their perfection. Only in the case of faith in Allah can the life of this world and the Hereafter be meaningful and purposeful. After the description of the attributes of the believers, why has the account of the stages of this wondrous development of life been brought here?

ولقد خلقنا الانسان من سللۃ من طین (23 : 12) "We created man from an extract of clay, then We made him a drop of fluid placed in a secure place." This verse describes the manner of human development with great precision. It shows that man reaches his present human form after passing through several stages. First he progressed from clay to man; mud, as it were, is the first stage of human creation, and man in his present form is the final stage of this process of creation. This is the reality that the Holy Qur'an expounds. We do not wish to confirm this process of human creation by those scientific observations which have observed this process of creation in great detail, showing how human life develops.

The Holy Qur'an has described how intricate creation is. The noteworthy point is how great the transformation is from mud to the creation of man. The Holy Qur'an has not given further details, because the purpose of the Qur'an is fulfilled by mentioning these broad stages of creation. As for present scientific observations, they set before us a very detailed account of the stages of development, so that they may explain in detail the stages from mud to the complete creation of man. Scientists' observations may be correct, and sometimes they also make erroneous observations. Today they state more stages, and tomorrow they reduce them, because observational instruments undergo changes from day to day.

The Qur'an sometimes describes these stages briefly and sometimes gives their details. Sometimes it contains just this phrase:

وبدا خلق الانسان من طین (32 : 7) "The initial creation of man was from clay." Now there is no mention of stages in this, while in the verse where details are given, it says:

من سللۃ من طین (23 : 12) "In the other verse, brevity has been employed." As for how man progressed from clay to his present complete state with continuity, the Qur'an has not given its details, and as we have given details elsewhere, these matters are not included among the aims of the Qur'an. The stages of life that the Qur'an has described may accord with scientific observations or may contradict them. It is also possible that this process occurred through some unknown means that man has not yet discovered, or that there are some factors that are beyond human knowledge. But the view with which the Qur'an regards man and the purposes for which these other scientific theories observe him are as different as earth from heaven. The Qur'an declares man to be a most honoured and chosen creature. It says that into this being Allah breathed His spirit, and it was this spirit that made him a human being from clay, and gave him two distinctive qualities by which he was called a human and was distinguished from animals. Thus the Qur'an's viewpoint regarding man is entirely distinct from that of materialists, and the word of Allah is truer than that of all people.

(See al-Insan bayn al-Maddiyya wal-Islam by Muhammad Qutb.) This is the original creation of the human species from an extract of clay. As for the subsequent line of human progeny, its manner is entirely different and is a well-known and observed method.

ثم جعلنہ نطفۃ فی قرار مکین (23 : 13) "Then We made him a drop of fluid in a secure place." Allah created the human species (Adam) from an extract of clay. As for the chain of procreation, Allah has set it in motion from a drop of water. This drop of water emerges from the male loins. It settles in the womb of the mother. It is an extremely tiny point of water, indeed one cell among thousands, and within this drop of water these cells are present in thousands.

فی قرار مکین (23 : 13) "in a secure place." This drop, upon reaching the womb, settles between the bones of the womb in such a place that the movements of the body have no effect upon it. It is a place which, while the back and stomach of a person receive jolts, blows, movements and impacts, is protected from them.

The Qur'an declares this point to be a stage of human creation; from this point, man becomes a complete human being. This is a scientific fact, yet it is a wondrous and worthy-of-reflection fact. When We reduce this great-bodied human being to this point, and within that point all the human characteristics are present, then from within a complete human being there continue to be created other such genes. This is a wondrous system of the chain of creation.

From this point, man then becomes an 'alaqa, that is, a clot of blood. In this stage, the male sperm combines with the female ovum, and initially this is a fine point suspended from the womb of the mother. This point receives nourishment from the blood of the mother's womb. From 'alaqa it then becomes al-mudgha, a "lump of flesh," in the form of a morsel. In the form of a morsel, this point is now somewhat larger. Now it is a piece of flesh. It is a thick piece of blood.

This small creature travels upon its path. It does not change its course, nor does it move away from its road. Its movement is orderly and arranged, and it accords with the law that Allah has set in advance, that is, in accordance with Allah's providence and decree. After this comes the stage of bones.

فخلقنا المضغۃ عظما (23 : 13) "Then We made the lump into bones." And after this stage came the stage in which flesh was clothed over the bones.

فکسونا العظم لحما (23 : 31) "Then We clothed the bones with flesh." On reading and then observing these stages, a person is astonished that the Qur'an has described these stages in such detail, which scientists observed much later. Later, scientists came to know that the cells of bones are different, and the cells of flesh are different, and it was established beyond doubt that within the embryo the bone cells are formed first, and afterwards flesh cells are laid upon them, and until the bone cells are complete, the flesh cells are not perfected, and afterwards the skeleton of the embryo is formed. This is an amazing reality, which the Qur'an records.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 23, verses 15–16:

﴿Then after that you will surely die.﴾ (23:15) ﴿Then on the Day of Resurrection you will surely be raised up.﴾ (23:16)

This death is the end of the life of this world, and it is also a stage between worldly life and the life of the Hereafter. Therefore, the life of the barzakh (the intermediate state between death and resurrection) is also a stage in the development of human life, and the barzakh is not the end of human life.

After this, man will be raised again, by the command of God. This too will be a period and a stage of life, but it will be a complete life. In that life there will be no deficiency, and it will not require the necessities of life of flesh and blood. In it there will be neither fear nor anxiety, nor any change, nor any ups and downs; rather, it will be a final resting place for man. But this complete life will be for the one who walks the paths of progress and perfection. He will have the life of those whose features have been determined in the opening verses of this surah, namely the life of the believers. But the one who did not develop the basic stage of his life, and instead brought it down to decline, making it like animal life, will, in the Hereafter too, be reversed in this manner. There his humanity will function like inanimate matter. He will become the fuel of Hell. And since the fuel of Hell is people and stones, such people will become stones even below the plants.

Now the context shifts from the internal proofs of faith in the human self to the proofs of faith present in the horizons of the universe. People see these universal proofs day and night, they even understand them well, yet they still pass by heedlessly.

The Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 23, verses 17–22:

Quran verses 17–22

The context presents these proofs and links them together, showing that all of them are signs of divine power. These signs also show the splendour and wise management with which this universe is run. These manifestations of creation are in harmony with one another; the functions and duties of these signs are also interconnected, and the direction they point to is also one: one Creator. All of them obey the one law of nature, cooperate with one another in their creative duties, and their services are all for this human being whom Allah has made honoured and dignified. For this reason, the creation of man and the other manifestations of nature are brought together here.

﴿And We have created above you seven paths, and We are not ever unaware of creation.﴾ (23:17) "And above you We created seven paths; and We were not unaware of creation." What are these seven paths (tara'iq)? They are in fact levels (tabaqat), some above others, or some very far from others. By "seven paths" may also be meant the great celestial orbits. Likewise, they may mean the seven galaxies, just as we live in the galaxy of the sun, or they may mean seven nebulae (sudam), and by sudam, in the view of astronomers, are meant clusters of stars (Nebulae). Whatever the meaning, these seven are celestial creations, and they are above human beings. In any case, these seven paths are high above the earth and are in this very expanse of the universe. Allah created them with His wise art, and Allah is not unaware of His creation.

﴿And We sent down from the sky water in measure, and We made it settle in the earth, and indeed We are able to take it away.﴾ (23:18) "And We sent down water from the sky in a measured quantity, and We caused it to settle in the earth; and We are certainly able to remove it." Here these seven paths join with the earth. Water descends from the sky. Water is connected with these seven heavens, because the fact that this universe was created in this manner is itself the guarantee that He sends water down from the heavens, and then this water settles upon the earth.

The theory that the water inside the earth is the water of rains, which seeps into the earth through various channels, is entirely a modern theory. Until the recent past, people thought that rainwater and the water inside the earth had no connection with each other, but the Quran had stated this reality about thirteen hundred years ago.

﴿And indeed We are able to take it away﴾ (23:18). All these matters relate to the proofs of faith, for those who have understanding, perception, thought and reflection, and who ponder over them; and all these matters are connected with the first and second paragraphs of this surah. Through these matters all the paragraphs become linked and harmonious.

If any one of these matters were absent, that is, water, ship, and wind, sea travel would become difficult. Even today sea travel is based on these same facilities.

All these matters relate to the proofs of faith, for those who have understanding, perception, thought and reflection, and who ponder over them; and all these matters are connected with the first and second paragraphs of this surah. Through these matters all the paragraphs become linked and harmonious.

Quran verses 17–22

The context presents these proofs and links them together, showing that all of them are signs of divine power. These signs also show the splendour and wise management with which this universe is run. These manifestations of creation are in harmony with one another; the functions and duties of these signs are also interconnected, and the direction they point to is also one: one Creator. All of them obey the one law of nature, cooperate with one another in their creative duties, and their services are all for this human being whom Allah has made honoured and dignified. For this reason, the creation of man and the other manifestations of nature are brought together here.

﴿And We have created above you seven paths, and We are not ever unaware of creation.﴾ (23:17) "And above you We created seven paths; and We were not unaware of creation." What are these seven paths (tara'iq)? They are in fact levels (tabaqat), some above others, or some very far from others. By "seven paths" may also be meant the great celestial orbits. Likewise, they may mean the seven galaxies, just as we live in the galaxy of the sun, or they may mean seven nebulae (sudam), and by sudam, in the view of astronomers, are meant clusters of stars (Nebulae). Whatever the meaning, these seven are celestial creations, and they are above human beings. In any case, these seven paths are high above the earth and are in this very expanse of the universe. Allah created them with His wise art, and Allah is not unaware of His creation.

﴿And We sent down from the sky water in measure, and We made it settle in the earth, and indeed We are able to take it away.﴾ (23:18) "And We sent down water from the sky in a measured quantity, and We caused it to settle in the earth; and We are certainly able to remove it." Here these seven paths join with the earth. Water descends from the sky. Water is connected with these seven heavens, because the fact that this universe was created in this manner is itself the guarantee that He sends water down from the heavens, and then this water settles upon the earth.

The theory that the water inside the earth is the water of rains, which seeps into the earth through various channels, is entirely a modern theory. Until the recent past, people thought that rainwater and the water inside the earth had no connection with each other, but the Quran had stated this reality about thirteen hundred years ago.

Then Allah sent down this water in exact measure: neither so much that it would drown everything in the form of a flood, nor so little that the lands would suffer drought and freshness and verdure would disappear. Nor did He send it out of season, so that the water would be wasted.
