This is also a kind of teaching for the believers who come after him, so that they do not sit back feeling secure against Allah's punishment and the stratagems of Satan. They should remain alert at all times and keep seeking refuge in Allah.

It is said that Allah has the power to bring the punishment upon them during the lifetime of Muhammad (ﷺ).

Wa innā ʿalā an nuriyaka mā naʿiduhum laqādirūn (23:95) "And indeed We are able to show you what We threaten them with." Allah showed the Prophet (ﷺ) a glimpse of this at the Battle of Badr. After that, a further aspect was shown at the Conquest of Makkah.

Idfaʿ billatī hiya aḥsan al-sayyiʾah naḥnu aʿlamu bimā yaṣifūn (23:96) "O Prophet, repel evil with that which is best; We know well what they attribute to you." At the time this surah was revealed, in Makkah, the method adopted for the call to Islam was to repel evil with good, to be patient until Allah's command arrives, and to leave matters to Allah.

The Prophet's (ﷺ) supplication, "O Lord, I seek refuge in You from the incitements of the devils," was made although he was under Allah's protection and was sinless. This is for greater caution and greater piety, for more earnest supplication to Allah, and for the sake of teaching the Ummah, since the Messenger himself is the model for his Ummah. In reality, this is a teaching for the Ummah that they should always seek Allah's protection from the incitements and whisperings of Satan. Rather, the Messenger (ﷺ) is directed to seek refuge from Satan's approach. Thus it is said:

Wa aʿūdhu bika rabbi an yaḥḍurūn (23:98) "Indeed, I seek refuge in You, O Lord, from their presence (approaching) me." It is also possible that at the time of death the Messenger (ﷺ) sought refuge from Satan appearing at that moment. The next verse, which is in the next lesson, also points to this.

Ḥattā idhā jāʾa aḥadahumu al-mawt (23:99) "Until, when death comes to one of them." This is the style of the Qur'an, in which one meaning flows harmoniously into another.

Ḥattā idhā ... yubʿathūn (23:99–100) "(These people will not give up their deeds) until, when death comes to one of them, he will say, 'My Lord, send me back, that I may do righteousness in what I have left behind.' Never! It is only a word he is saying. Behind them is a barrier (barzakh) until the Day they are resurrected."

In this final lesson too, the discussion of the evil end of the polytheists continues. Now these people are within one of the scenes of the Day of Resurrection. It begins from the time of the taking of souls at the beginning of the world and ends with the blowing of the Trumpet. At the end of the surah, returning to the main theme, they are warned not to call upon anyone else alongside Allah, for there is no deity but Allah. The surah concludes with the guidance that the Messenger (ﷺ) himself should seek forgiveness from Allah.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 23, verse 99:

Until, when death comes to one of them, he says, "My Lord, send me back, (23:99) so that I may do righteous work in what I have left behind." (23:100)

This scene is that of the throes of death. When death comes, every person repents; he turns back to Allah and makes this request: "O Allah, grant me one more chance, give me one more life, so that we may correct those shortcomings and dispose of the family and wealth we have left behind in accordance with Your will." This is a scene that everyone witnesses, and the one who is dying makes this request, and it is still openly made even now.

﴿Nay, it is but a word he utters﴾ (23:100). "No, never! It is merely a word that he is saying." It is a statement he is making, and nothing corresponding to it will come into existence. Neither the words nor the one who speaks them deserve any consideration. This is merely a cry that escapes the mouth in a state of fear. It is not based on sincerity, nor is it genuine repentance. Everyone says such things in times of difficulty; there is no such thing in the heart, nor is there any intention behind it.

Now the state of the throes of death comes to an end. A barrier, a barrier (barzakh) comes between the one who says this and the world. The matter is over. Relationships have ended. Doors have closed and curtains have fallen.

The passage contains a Qur'anic quotation which I should render. The text "ومن ۔۔۔۔ یبعثون (23 : 100)" is an elided quotation, so I'll keep it as it stands, with the translated verse-reference, and translate the commentary.

Wa min wara'ihim barzakhun ila yawmi yub'athun (23:100) ﴿And before them is a barrier (barzakh) until the Day they are raised.﴾

Barzakh (the intervening barrier) means a screen lies between them. They are neither of the people of this world nor of the people of the Hereafter. They are in the realm of this barzakh, and these people will remain here until the establishment of the Resurrection. Now the context of the discourse enters the Resurrection, at the time when the Trumpet is blown.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 23, verse 101:

Fa-idha... wa la yatasa'aluna (101): All bonds will be severed. The values by which they lived their lives in the world will cease to exist.

Fa-la... yawma'idhin (23:101): "On that Day there will be no kinship between them." Such dread will overtake them that all will be silent. They will stand mute, and no one will speak. Now the balance of reckoning is presented here with great swiftness and brevity.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 23, verses 102–104:

"Then as for those whose scales are heavy..." to "...grinning with their lips drawn back" (23:102–104). This too is a particular feature of the Qur'an's style: it presents any meaning in a tangible, sensory form so that even the most abstract ideas are understood by every person.

Consider further, along with these deeds, that the fire will lick the flesh from their faces, and they will appear as the jawbones of a dead person appear, with their teeth bared.

These are the people whose scale of deeds has become light. They have lost everything; they have lost even their own selves. When a person loses his very life, what does he remain the master of? What remains in his possession? He has lost his self; his being has gone. It is as if his very existence no longer remains.

Now the narrative style suddenly changes and direct address begins. They are rebuked. Physical punishment is not as painful as this rebuke is torturous. Now, as it were, we are once again seeing a scene in which they are being reprimanded and censured.

Ayah 23:105: "Were not My verses recited to you, and did you not deny them?"

When they heard this question, it occurred to them that perhaps they had been granted permission to speak and could give an answer, and that perhaps the acknowledgement of their sins might benefit them.

**Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 23, verses 106–107:**

"They will say: 'Our Lord, our misfortune overcame us, and we were a people astray. Our Lord, bring us out of it; then if we return [to disbelief], we will indeed be wrongdoers.'" (Qur'an 23:106–107)

This is an extremely bitter confession, and their wretchedness is plainly evident in it. They overstepped their limits and committed a breach of proper conduct, since they were only permitted to answer a question. Indeed, it is also possible that this question was asked merely to humiliate them, and that no answer was actually sought. Therefore their request is answered harshly, because no request had been asked of them.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 23, verse 108:

Qal... wa la tukallimun ("He said: ...and do not speak to Me"). Be silent! Adopt the silence of a humiliated person. You fully deserve the punishment in which you are caught. This is the most fitting position for you.

Verses 109–110: "Indeed, there was a group of My servants who said, 'Our Lord, we have believed, so forgive us and have mercy upon us, and You are the best of the merciful.' But you took them in mockery, until they caused you to forget My remembrance, and you used to laugh at them."

Your crime is not merely that you disbelieved and kept yourselves in disbelief. Although that too was a great crime, you have committed an even greater one: you made mockery of those who believed. Those who had faith and sought the mercy of their Lord, you used to ridicule, and in this way you deprived yourselves of the remembrance of Allah and of the lessons of admonition, although the signs of faith were present in this universe. Look now at your own standing, and at the rank and status of those whom you used to mock.

The passage you have given is a fragment of the Urdu translation, and it begins and ends mid-argument. Here is its translation:

"Indeed, I have rewarded them this day for their patience, that they are the ones who are triumphant." After this harsh and insulting answer, a new cycle of question and answer begins, and in this exchange they are treated with great contempt and are rendered speechless. Now a new question comes.

Say, "How many years did you remain on earth?" (Qur'an 23:112)

The verse begins with the question addressed to the people of the Fire, and the commentary follows. Allah certainly knows well how long they spent in the world, but the purpose here is to show how brief this worldly life is, how insignificant, and how short its days are. They sacrificed the eternal life of the Hereafter for this short worldly life. Today they feel how short the world was, and how fleeting it was, yet they are in despair and their hearts are constricted. Now, what concern do they have to reckon?

﴿They said, "We remained …" … "… so ask those who count."﴾

This is the answer of a person who is extremely anxious, despondent and distressed.

But the answer is most realistic: you spent a very short time compared to the time you will spend in Hell. If only you had made a correct assessment while in the world.

Once again they are rebuked, and at the same time it is explained what the wisdom behind resurrection after death is: ﴿Say: If you had remained [in the earth] but a little, if only you had known...﴾ [Qur'an 23:112–114, partially quoted]. Here "ba'th ba'd al-mawt" (resurrection after death) is the subject.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 23, verse 115:

"Did you think that We created you without purpose, and that you would not be returned to Us?" [23:115] It should be understood that wisdom necessarily requires that there be resurrection after death. Allah, the Exalted, has decreed its establishment. Its purposes are part of the governance of the universe. The Last Day is the logical outcome of creation. With resurrection, the creation of the universe reaches its perfection and the purpose of creation is fulfilled. Only those people can be heedless of this truth whose hearts have been covered with veils and whose natural disposition has become distorted, who never take the trouble to reflect upon the wisdom of Allah, although this wisdom lies scattered throughout this universe.

The Surah concludes with the proclamation of the belief in the Oneness of Allah (tawhid), and it is announced that those who committed shirk have fallen into great loss, while the people of tawhid will attain success. The Prophet (ﷺ) is directed to seek forgiveness from Allah and to beg for the mercy of Allah.

Fa-ta'ala Allahu... al-Malik al-Haqq... la ilaha illa Huwa Rabbu al-'Arsh al-Karim (23:116)... [The Qur'anic quotations here are cited in the source at 23:116 and 23:118]. Before this, the scene of the Day of Resurrection has passed. This is a comment upon it. Also, in the earlier scenes, debate and argument, with clear proofs and evidence, had been detailed. This comment is the logical conclusion of this entire surah: that Allah is free from shirk. He is the true Owner, the supreme Sovereign, and there is no deity besides Him. Sovereignty belongs to Him, and He alone deserves exaltation. He is the Lord of the Mighty Throne.

Now, those who acknowledge the divinity and sovereignty of any personality other than Allah have no justification for it. There is no proof of it in this universe, human nature does not accept it, and human reason does not incline toward it. Those who make such a claim will have to give account before their Lord, and the outcome of that accountability is simply this: the disbelievers never attain success. This is the Sunnah of Allah, and it is unalterable. In contrast, the people of faith will attain success, and this is the demand of human nature and the demand of the order of the universe.

As for the disbelievers' possessions, the worldly provisions and the worldly power that sometimes continues to be established for them, this is not their success. It is a trial and a test for them. If some of them depart from this world without accountability, then accountability awaits them in the Hereafter, where they will have to give a full and complete account. The Hereafter will be the final scene of this creation. In the system of Allah's creation, the Hereafter is not separate or distant from this world. It is the final page of this world and a part of it.

In the final verse of Surah al-Mu'minun, the Prophet (ﷺ) is directed to keep seeking the forgiveness and mercy of Allah: "And say, 'My Lord, forgive and have mercy, and You are the best of the merciful'" (23:118). Notice that the beginning and the end of the surah converge on the same theme. The beginning also deals with the theme that the believers succeeded and the disbelievers fell into loss. At the beginning there was also the theme of humility and submissiveness in prayer, and here too there is supplication and the seeking of mercy before Allah. Thus the beginning and end of the surah become alike.
